passage: Mehak had heard that Sonali, a senior, loved old film songs, so by Wednesday her playlist was full of them. In the lunch line she stood two places behind Sonali and memorised everything she said: the joke about the physics teacher, the way she pushed her hair back, her opinion on mangoes. Everything Sonali said felt like a small gift. It was wonderful, like walking around lit from inside. When the dance rehearsal clashed with the library hour Sonali used, Mehak told the choreographer she was ill. That evening her friend Simran said, "You've missed two practices, and you don't even like those songs." Mehak went quiet. Then she saw Sonali on the stairs, arguing with her phone charger and looking simply tired. She wasn't a film star. She was a person. Mehak went back to rehearsal on Friday.

qa.q: What did Mehak fill her playlist with because of Sonali?
qa.a: She filled it with old film songs, because she had heard Sonali loved them.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling as she memorised Sonali's every word?
qa.a: Thrilled and dazzled. Everything Sonali said felt like a small gift, and it was like walking around lit from inside.

qa.q: What helped Mehak get her own life going again?
qa.a: Simran pointed out the missed practices, and seeing Sonali tired with a phone charger showed her a normal person. So she went back to rehearsal on Friday.

qa.q: How might Simran see Mehak's behaviour?
qa.a: She is probably worried. She says Mehak has missed two practices for songs she does not even like, so she sees her changing herself for someone else.

grounding: Mehak sees her crush as flawless and hangs on her words, then remembers Sonali is ordinary and returns to her own activities.

passage:
Last year, Hafsa was the most perfect person I had ever seen. At least that's what I believed.
She sat two rows ahead in English. When she said a poem was beautiful, I went home and read it three times. She liked a band I'd never heard of; within a week I knew all their songs. I stopped going to football practice because it clashed with the drama club she'd joined, and I don't even like drama.
It felt wonderful. Every day had a glow.
Then one afternoon I heard her snap at a junior for bumping her tray, really sharply. I felt oddly shocked. She was just a person. A nice one, mostly, and sometimes grumpy, like everyone.
I went back to football. I kept the band, because honestly I like them now. And I still smile when Hafsa laughs. I'm Anand, and I'm just a bit less blind now.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa sit in English?
How did Anand feel when Hafsa snapped at the junior?
qa.a: Anand felt oddly shocked, realising Hafsa was an ordinary person rather than someone perfect.

qa.q: What steps helped Anand keep a life of Anand's own?
qa.a: Returning to football practice, keeping only the interests Anand truly liked, and enjoying the crush without rebuilding everything around Hafsa.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Anand, if she noticed?
qa.a: Hafsa may not know how much Anand admired her; she might see a friendly classmate from English and drama club.

grounding: A teen who sees a crush as flawless and rebuilds life around her realises she is ordinary and returns to their own interests.

passage:
Science teacher's note, Class 11, 12 September
Nirmala has been one of our most curious students all year. For the inter-school science fair, she proposed a water filter model and was excited about it.
Over the past three weeks, I've noticed a change. She started joining Dhruv's drama rehearsals every lunch. In class she quotes him often and laughs at everything he says, even small comments. On Monday she told me she'd drop the filter project to help paint his play's backdrop.
Today I asked her to stay back. I didn't mention Dhruv. I asked how she felt about the filter. She said, "I love it. But it's not that important." Then she stopped and said, "Actually, it is."
We agreed she'd keep the filter project and paint on weekends only. She laughed and said, "He's not a god, is he." I said no, just a nice classmate. I'll check in on the project Friday.

qa.q: What model did Nirmala propose for the science fair?
What does Nirmala's pause before saying 'Actually, it is' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels torn and a little embarrassed, realising she had been ready to drop something she loves because of her crush.

qa.q: How did the note-writer help Nirmala keep her own life going?
qa.a: By asking about her project instead of Dhruv, letting her reach her own answer, and agreeing on a plan that keeps both.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Nirmala's constant attention?
qa.a: He may enjoy it or feel a little awkward, but he likely doesn't know she nearly gave up her own project for his play.

grounding: A teen idolises her crush and almost gives up her own project for him, and a teacher helps her see him as an ordinary person.
